title: The last four petitions (CCC 2828–2854)

lines: NOW THE PRAYER TURNS TO US.
cards: The Douay-Rheims Bible gives the same bread two different names. In Luke, the Our Father asks, "Give us this day our daily bread."
Turn back to Matthew, same prayer, and it reads, "Give us this day our supersubstantial bread." Supersubstantial. Nobody says that at the bakery.
It isn't a typo, and it isn't careless. It sits right on a real puzzle in the prayer, and the Catechism walks straight into it. The prayer has turned toward God three times.
Now it turns toward us. Today: the last four petitions.

teach.h: GIVE: BREAD FOR TODAY, AND MORE.
teach.b: Give. The Catechism notes that the Greek word behind daily, epiousios, appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Read one way, it points to time: bread for this day, enough for now.

Read more literally, it points beyond ordinary bread, to the bread of life, which Catholics understand as Christ himself in the Eucharist. The Church keeps both: bread for the table, and bread for the soul. Forgive.
"And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors." The Catechism calls this petition astonishing, and leans on the small word as. God's mercy can't get into a heart that refuses to forgive.
Not because the mercy is small, but because a closed heart is closed.
Lead. "And lead us not into temptation." Does God lead anyone into temptation?

The letter of James answers flatly: "God is not a tempter of evils, and he tempteth no man." The Catechism says the Greek carries two shades: don't let us enter into temptation, and don't let us give in to it. Deliver.
"But deliver us from evil." Here, the Catechism says, evil isn't only an idea.

It names a person, the evil one, who opposes God, and reads the petition as asking to be freed from all evil, past, present and future, of which he is the author. Give, forgive, lead, deliver. Four requests, all plural.

how: Catholics pray these petitions in every Our Father; at Mass it is said just before Communion, and some hear 'our daily bread' there as pointing to the Eucharist as well as ordinary food.

games.q: what does “the last four petitions” mean?
o: the four Gospels, read in turn through the year
four rules for receiving Communion worthily
the Our Father's asks for bread, mercy and rescue

games.q: give, forgive, lead, deliver — tap the pairs.
p: mercy can't enter a heart that won't forgive
evil as a person, not only an idea

s: the Douay-Rheims says daily bread in Luke and supersubstantial bread in Matthew
the same petition, two renderings of one puzzling Greek word, epiousios.
lead us not into temptation means God tempts people
James: "God is not a tempter of evils, and he tempteth no man." the Catechism says the Greek means don't let us enter, or give in.
the Catechism treats evil in this petition as only an idea
it says evil here is a person, the evil one, who opposes God.

games.q: you're translating "give us this day our ___ bread," and the Greek word appears nowhere else in the New Testament. what does the Catholic tradition do with it?
o: pick ordinary daily bread, and drop the rest.
pick only the Eucharist, and drop the rest.
keep both: bread for today, and the bread of life.
games.why: the Catechism holds both senses: bread for this day, and, read literally, the bread of life, Christ in the Eucharist.

practice: Ask yourself what you actually need for today, not this year, just today: food, maybe, or patience, or one honest conversation, or rest. Then think of one other person who needs bread today, of any kind.
If you pray, say "Give us this day our daily bread" with both of you in the us; if you don't, hold the two needs side by side.

wordCard.voice: The last four petitions. In the Our Father: give us bread, forgive us as we forgive, lead us not into temptation, deliver us from evil.

orig.note: Greek: the word in the bread petition, rendered daily, and in the Douay-Rheims Matthew, supersubstantial.
